issues.legal_issue: A court cannot enter judgment against a defendant solely because no written statement was filed without considering whether the plaint supports judgment or whether facts require proof.
material_facts: The defendants did not file a written statement despite receiving time and a further opportunity to do so.
The suit was decreed under Order 8 Rule 10 because of the defendants’ failure to file a written statement.
The plaint itself disclosed a material factual dispute about whether the defendants had obtained and sent the required tax permission to the plaintiff.
issues.conclusion: The decree could not properly be entered merely because the written statement was not filed; the court had to consider the plaint and determine whether any facts required proof, and could instead make another appropriate order.
issues.legal_principle: Order 8 Rules 5(2) and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure permit judgment on the plaint or another appropriate order when no written statement is filed, but preserve the court’s discretion to require proof. Order 12 Rule 6 and Section 58 of the Evidence Act likewise allow a court to require proof despite admissions. The court relied on Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah, which explains the judicial discretion under Order 8 Rule 10, and Razia Begum v. Sahebzadi Anwar Begum, which recognizes that admissions do not invariably dispense with proof.

predicates.defendant_filed_no_written_statement: The defendant did not file a written statement in the civil suit.
predicates.plaint_discloses_material_factual_disput: The plaintiff’s own pleading discloses a material factual dispute relevant to deciding the claim.

issues.definition: When a defendant has not filed a written statement but the plaint discloses a material factual dispute, the court does not decree the suit solely for that failure.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment must state the material facts, the controversy resolved, and the reasoning for the decision, including when the case is decided after a defendant fails to file a written statement.
material_facts: The trial court decreed the suit in a brief order that focused on the defendants’ failure to file a written statement and did not set out the facts or reasoning supporting the decree.
The appellate court affirmed the decree without addressing the material factual dispute disclosed by the plaint.
issues.conclusion: The judgments were legally deficient because they did not set out the facts, controversy, and reasoning supporting the decision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure defines a judgment as a statement of the grounds for a decree or order; Order 20 Rule 4(2) requires a concise statement of the case, points for determination, decisions, and reasons. These requirements apply to contested cases, ex parte cases, and cases decided under Order 8 Rule 10. The court relied on Nanhe v. Saiyad Tasadduq Husain, Thippaiah v. Kuri Obaiah, and Dineshwar Prasad Bakshi v. Parmeshwar Prasad Sinha.

predicates.civil_judgment_is_pronounced: A court pronounces a judgment in a civil proceeding.

issues.definition: Whenever a civil judgment is pronounced, it states the case, the controversy, the decision, and the reasons for that decision.

issues.legal_issue: A decree for specific performance cannot be entered on deemed admissions without examining whether the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform when the pleadings disclose a material factual dispute bearing on that requirement.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought specific performance of an agreement that required the defendants to obtain tax permission and send it to him before he paid a further part of the sale price.
The plaintiff alleged that the permission had not been obtained or sent, while also pleading that the defendants asserted that they had obtained and sent it.
The dispute about obtaining and sending the permission could bear on whether the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform his part of the agreement.
issues.conclusion: The disputed facts bearing on readiness and willingness had to be proved; the court could not decree specific performance merely because the defendants had filed no written statement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Specific Relief Act requires the plaintiff in a specific-performance suit to plead and establish readiness and willingness to perform. Under Order 8 Rules 5(2) and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may require proof of facts despite deemed admissions. The court also relied on Razia Begum v. Sahebzadi Anwar Begum and Section 58 of the Evidence Act concerning the court’s discretion to require proof of admitted facts.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brings a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.pleadings_disclose_dispute_material_to_r: The pleadings disclose a material factual dispute that bears on whether the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, when the pleadings disclose a material dispute bearing on readiness and willingness, the court requires proof of the relevant facts.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may exercise its discretionary appellate jurisdiction to correct a legally deficient judgment involving an important question of law despite the parties’ procedural misconduct.
material_facts: The defendants had delayed filing their written statement and their appeal to the High Court was also late.
A sale deed had been executed in the plaintiff’s favour through a court-appointed commissioner.
The case raised an important legal question about what a court must do when a written statement is not filed, and the judgments below were deficient.
issues.conclusion: The Court exercised its discretion to allow the appeal, set aside the judgments below, and remand the case for a fresh decision.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers discretionary jurisdiction; the Court stated that it is not bound to interfere merely because a judgment is incorrect, but exercised that jurisdiction because an important legal question required determination and the judgments could not be sustained.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: A party brings an appeal invoking the Supreme Court’s discretionary appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.important_legal_question: The appeal presents an important legal question requiring determination.
predicates.material_legal_deficiency: The judgment under appeal has a material legal deficiency.

issues.definition: When an appeal raises an important legal question and the judgment has a material legal deficiency, the Supreme Court may intervene despite party misconduct.
